leo.name: Low Earth Orbit
leo.period: About 90 minutes at very low altitude; varies with height
leo.purpose: Close passes support detailed observation and research.
leo.applications: Earth imaging, science missions, crewed spacecraft
leo.advantages: High-detail views and relatively short signal distance.
leo.limitations: The satellite moves quickly over the surface; a location is visible only during a pass.

sso.name: Sun-Synchronous Orbit
sso.altitude: Often several hundred km; Terra example: 705 km
sso.purpose: A near-polar orbit whose plane precesses to keep a similar local solar time for repeat passes.
sso.advantages: Consistent lighting can help compare images collected on different days.
sso.limitations: SSO is generally a special near-polar LEO, not a separate altitude class. Lighting consistency is approximate and mission-specific.
sso.missionFit: Excellent fit for repeated Earth-surface observations.

meo.name: Medium Earth Orbit
meo.purpose: A middle-altitude region that gives broad coverage over a larger area.
meo.applications: Navigation satellite constellations such as GPS
meo.advantages: Broader coverage per satellite than LEO.
meo.limitations: Less detailed surface imaging than a closer orbit; a single satellite cannot provide continuous global coverage.
meo.missionFit: Limited fit for detailed Earth imaging; useful as a navigation-orbit example.

geo.name: Geostationary Orbit
geo.purpose: An equatorial circular orbit that matches Earth’s rotation, appearing fixed over one longitude.
geo.advantages: Continuous view of a large region from one spacecraft.
geo.limitations: Farther distance means less surface detail; polar regions are poorly covered.
geo.missionFit: Suited to continuous regional monitoring, less suited to fine-detail surface imaging.
